t.1.149.1: Kuntī said: You must by no means give way to despair because of this danger. A way has been found here for deliverance from that Rākṣasa.
t.1.149.3: I have five sons, O brahmin; one of them will go for your sake, taking the offering to that wicked rākṣasa.
t.1.149.4: I will by no means do this out of a desire to live: the parting of a brahmin, and a guest at that, from his life for my own sake.
t.1.149.2: You have only one son, a mere boy, and only one daughter, a poor girl; I do not approve of either of them going there, nor of your wife.
t.1.149.5: But this is not found among women of low birth, nor among the most unrighteous: that one would give up oneself and even one's own son for the sake of a brahmin.
t.1.149.6: But I resolve that I must discern what is truly best for my own self: between the slaying of a brahmin and the slaying of oneself, the slaying of myself is better for me.
t.1.149.7: The killing of a brahmin is the highest sin, and there is no atonement for it even when it is committed unknowingly. Better for me is the killing of myself.
t.1.149.10: To abandon one who has come to one's house, and likewise one who seeks refuge, and to kill one who begs for mercy, is held to be the utmost cruelty.
t.1.149.8: But I do not desire my own death by my own hand, O fair lady; when the killing is done by others, no sin whatsoever attaches to me.
t.1.149.9: Should that slaying of a brahmin be brought about by me with deliberate intent, I see no atonement for it; it would be cruel and base indeed.
t.1.149.12: Better indeed is my own destruction this very day, together with my wife; I will by no means consent to the killing of a brāhmaṇa.
t.1.149.11: One should never do a blameworthy deed, nor a cruel one: so the great-souled ancients, who knew the law for times of distress, understood.
t.1.149.14: That Rākṣasa is not able to bring about the destruction of my son, for my son is mighty, perfected in mantras, and full of splendor.
t.1.149.13: I too, O brahmin, hold this firm conviction, that brahmins must be protected. Yet no son of mine is unloved by me, even if I were to have a hundred sons.
t.1.149.15: He will deliver all that food to the Rākṣasa and will also set himself free; such is my firm conviction.
t.1.149.16: Rākṣasas have been met by the hero and seen by him before, and many times those mighty, huge-bodied ones have also been slain.
t.1.149.19: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by Pṛthā, the brahmin, together with his wife, was delighted and honored those words, which were like amṛta.
t.1.149.17: But this must by no means be told to anyone, O brahmin, for out of curiosity people would harass my sons, who are seekers of knowledge.
t.1.149.18: Whomever my son, without leave from his teacher, should cause to learn it, that person could not accomplish his task by means of that knowledge; such is the view of the good.
t.1.149.20: Then Kuntī and the brahmin together said to him, the son of the Wind, "Do it," and he said to them both, "So be it."
